concept_posts.post_content:
Ever tried to compare sales numbers from Redshift with marketing spend stored in S3?

I ran into that last week,
and it reminded me how QuickSight handles joins and blending.

In QuickSight a join is just like a SQL join inside a single dataset.
You pull both tables into the same data source,
and then define the keys you want to match.
The result is a combined view you can use for charts.

Blending is different.
It lets you link two separate datasets – say Redshift and S3 – without moving the data.
QuickSight creates a virtual relationship at query time.
This is handy when the sources are large or you don’t have permission to copy them.

Key takeaways:
- Joins work when the tables share the same data source.
- Blending lets you combine tables from different sources on the fly.
- Pick the right join type – inner,
 left,
 right – to keep the records you need.

Common mistake: using blending for everything.
It adds latency and can hide mismatched keys.
Instead, use a join if the data can reside in one source.

How do you decide between a join and a blend for your dashboards?

concept_posts.post_content:
Ever wonder why some rows in your dimension table seem to change over time while others stay the same?

I ran into this when cleaning up a customer master for a retail client.

The pattern is called Slowly Changing Dimensions or SCD for short.

Think of a customer address that can move.

If you store the latest address only,
 you lose history.

If you keep every address change as a new row,
 you preserve history but your queries get more complex.

That trade‑off is what the different SCD types address.

For example, Type 1 simply overwrites the old value.

Type 2 adds a new row with start and end dates.

Type 3 adds a new column to hold the previous value.

Key takeaways:

- Choose Type 1 for corrections that don’t need audit.
- Use Type 2 when you need full history for reporting.
- Type 3 is handy for keeping a single “previous” snapshot without row explosion.

A common mistake is mixing types in the same table without clear documentation,
 which leads to confusing query results.

Which SCD type have you found most useful in your projects?
